records.name: Konrad
records.facts_used: Konrad is a Conrad-family form with Germanic kuoni, bold, and rat, counsel. The name guide documents it in several European language traditions. This family origin remains distinct from the life story of a particular Estonian painter. Kumu Art Museum’s Konrad Mägi exhibition ran from 24 August 2018 to 24 March 2019. It showed more than forty paintings, focusing on landscapes and including works from his Italian period. Eero Epner curated it.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: The name guide explicitly relates Konrad and Conrad. The Kumu exhibition dates, more-than-forty-paintings scope and curator were checked against the museum’s own page.

records.name: Kuno
records.facts_used: The name guide connects Kuno with short forms of Germanic names in kunni, clan or family; it can also shorten Konrad. Both relationships remain distinct, without choosing one route for every Estonian bearer. Kuno Pajula was elected archbishop of the Estonian Evangelical Lutheran Church on 11 June 1987 and retired in 1994. He was also a founder of the Estonian Council of Churches and its president in 1989–1993.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: Germanic kunni-family and Konrad-shortening accounts remain distinct. Pajula’s election, retirement and council service are historical statements from the church’s own biography, not current-office claims.

records.name: Kuuno
records.facts_used: The Estonian dictionary entry connects Kuuno with a diminutive of Konrad and lists Kuno alongside it. This is a direct language-specific reference, not a relationship inferred from the doubled vowel alone. The two spellings’ historical records still remain distinct. A 2021 Pärnu heritage inventory documents architect Kuuno Raude’s 1993 building as a local example of postmodernism, noting its independent architectural value. Here Kuuno is the architect’s personal name, not a place or company name.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: The exact Estonian dictionary entry explicitly gives the Konrad diminutive and related Kuno. The heritage PDF page 89 row was visually inspected and identifies architect Kuuno Raude and a 1993 building. No resident information or private address is published.

records.name: Alvilė
records.facts_used: Official name data classify Alvilė as a Lithuanian compound. A popular name guide proposes al- linked with each and vil- with viltis, hope. This is the guide’s origin proposal, not the one independently demonstrated meaning of the compound. Children’s writer Alvilė Rimaitė visited Tauragė’s Aušros school on 10–11 November 2025. The school’s own report describes a reading about Kliukliukas and a workshop making the character from yarn, a documented literary event involving a real bearer.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: The official registry establishes compound-name classification. The popular guide’s al-/vil- interpretation is attributed as a proposal, not independently proven. The school’s primary report was published 15 November 2025 and dates the author’s visit to 10–11 November 2025. A similarly named company was rejected as personal-name evidence.

records.name: Kristinas
records.facts_used: Linguist Antanas Salys explains Latin Christinus as a variant of Christianus, linking the Kristinas family with the designation Christian. This is a specific relationship between forms, distinct from the similarly beginning name Kristupas. Kristinas Astikas was a witness to the Treaty of Salynas in 1398 and the Union of Horodło in 1413. The Lithuanian encyclopaedia identifies him as founder of the Astikas family; his son Radvila founded the Radvila family.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: Salys explicitly treats Christinus as a Christianus variant; ultimate Greek and intermediate Latin stages are not contradictory. VLE documents Kristinas Astikas as witness to the 1398 and 1413 agreements. Kristupas is a separate form.

records.name: Renata
records.facts_used: Renata is the feminine of Latin Renatus, explained as born again. The international name guide explicitly includes Lithuanian usage of Renata. This family meaning is not a claim about events in any particular person’s life. Renata Šerelytė’s first short-story book, Žuvies darinėjimas, appeared in Vilnius in 1995. Her novel Vardas tamsoje became the basis of Agnė Marcinkevičiūtė’s 2013 film. The Writers’ Union biography documents this passage from book to screen.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: The feminine Renatus relationship and Lithuanian usage are explicit. The 1995 book and 2013 adaptation come from the Writers’ Union biography; no current residence claim is included.

records.name: Teodoras
records.facts_used: Teodoras is a Lithuanian form in the Greek Theodoros family. Its elements are theos, god, and dōron, gift, traditionally gift of God. The related Dorothea uses the same elements in the reverse order. Historian Teodoras Narbutas published his extensive history of Lithuania in Polish in nine volumes in 1835–1841. Its first volume concerned ancient mythology. This records his publication, rather than endorsing every historical or mythological interpretation in it.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: The direct Lithuanian guide supplies the Greek elements. The attempted Wiktionary #Lithuanian source actually contained only a Portuguese plural and was rejected, as was a user-submitted-only Behind the Name entry. Narbutas’s nine-volume publication is documented without endorsing his historical or mythological conclusions.

records.name: Kaija
records.facts_used: The dictionary compares Kaija with Latvian kaija, seagull, and separately lists it as a Finnish form of Katarīna. These are different linguistic connections. The pure interpretation under Katarīna is not automatically Kaija’s only meaning. The catalogue gives a personal-name attestation of Kaija in 1549 and a calendar entry in 1910. These are different historical layers. Calendar inclusion does not date the form’s creation, and the early record alone does not choose between the two origin accounts.
records.reason: An opened reference and a concrete dated dictionary, archival, cultural or professional record support a reviewed account.
records.uncertainties: The Latvian seagull comparison and Finnish Katarīna relationship remain distinct; pure is not asserted as the only meaning.

records.name: Kornelijs
records.facts_used: The Polish-name rendering manual gives Kornelijs and Kornēlijs together for Korneli, directly documenting their relationship. The catalogue links Kornēlijs to Roman Cornelius; further comparisons with cornu, horn, or the tree word cornus remain tentative. For the macron spelling Kornēlijs specifically, the catalogue gives a 1638 attestation near Valmiera and a calendar entry in 1767. These dates remain attached to Kornēlijs. The manual’s paired forms alone do not prove Kornelijs in those same early years.

records.uncertainties: The Polish rendering manual PDF page 33 (printed page 51) explicitly pairs Korneli with Kornelijs and *Kornēlijs; the table was visually inspected.
